newsitem.title: POLAND: Russia warns Poland over NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Russia warns Poland over NATO membership.

text.p: The Russian parliamentary chief, repeating Moscow's opposition to NATO enlargement, warned Poland on Tuesday that his country would step up military spending if the pact recruited new members from Central Europe.

"NATO enlargement will force Russia to change its national security doctrine and... increase military spending," Gennady Seleznyov, the speaker of Russia's State Duma, told Polish parliamentarians in a meeting in Warsaw.

"For example, we would have to reconstruct our already buried programme of medium-range bombers," he said. He reiterated the Duma was also unlikely to ratify the START-2 treaty on nuclear arms reduction if NATO grew.

Last week, about 150 members of the Duma formed a group dedicated to safeguarding the country against NATO expansion to the east, which said it may stall ratification of nuclear and conventional arms treaties.

Seleznyov, winding down a three-day visit of Russian parliamentarians, said Moscow especially opposed any deployment of the Western pact's troops and military equipment onto new members' territory, notably stationing of nuclear arms there.

A future deal between Russia and NATO, which Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana are due to discuss on February 23 in Brussels, should provide for safeguards against such moves, he said.
He said the deal should have the form of a treaty to make sure that it would be implemented.
"During talks on German unification...we were assured that NATO would not be enlarged and this proved to be words only.... Moscow does not believe words any more," he said.
Seleznyov also said that apart from sharp differences over the NATO expansion, relation between Russia and Poland were good and economic co-operation should be boosted.

"We will not see enemies in Poland, Hungary and other countries seeking NATO membership. Our society understands that even if three or five Nato's are created we will have enough power to respond to them," he said.

NATO has said it will invite the first former members of the defunct Soviet-led Warsaw Pact for talks on membership during its Madrid summit in July. Poland, along with the Czech Republic and Hungary, hope to join the pact by 1999.

Seleznyov, calling NATO "a relic of the Cold War," repeated Russia's calls for the creation of a new security system in Europe based on the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).

NATO and other analysts have repeatedly said the OCSE is too weak and its operations too uncoordinated to be able to ensure stability and peace on the continent and Poland says it wants nothing short of full NATO membership.
